Introduction

Can a person actually be born with three nostrils?

Yes — although it is extremely rare.

A supernumerary nostril, also called an accessory nostril, is a rare congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal embryological development of the nasal structures.

Instead of having only the two normal external nasal openings, an individual may develop an additional opening on the nose. The internal anatomy of this accessory opening can vary considerably between individuals.

What Is a Supernumerary Nostril?

During embryological development, the structures that form the nose undergo a highly coordinated process of growth, fusion, and differentiation.

Disturbances in these developmental processes can occasionally result in congenital nasal anomalies, including a supernumerary nostril.

Published case reports have documented individuals with triple nostrils, and exceptionally rare cases with multiple additional nasal openings have also been described.

Does the Third Nostril Actually Connect to the Nasal Cavity?

This is one of the most interesting aspects of the condition.

The additional external opening may have different internal anatomical configurations.

In some cases, the accessory nostril communicates with the normal nasal cavity through a narrow patent tract. When such a communication is present, some airflow may pass through the additional opening.

In other cases, the tract terminates blindly and does not communicate with the main nasal airway.

Therefore, simply seeing an additional external opening does not tell us whether it is functionally connected to the nasal cavity.

What Happens Inside a Blind-Ending Accessory Nostril?

A blind-ending accessory nostril is not necessarily just an empty hole.

The tract may have different types of epithelial lining depending on the developmental characteristics of that particular anomaly. Some reported accessory tracts contain respiratory-type mucosa, while others may have skin-like epithelium and associated structures.

Because of these differences, secretions can occur in some accessory tracts.

If a tract contains mucosal tissue capable of producing secretions but has no normal drainage pathway into the nasal cavity, secretions may accumulate within the blind-ending tract.

Over time, this can potentially result in mucus accumulation and crust formation at or around the external opening.

However, this does not mean that every blind-ending accessory nostril will produce mucus or crusting. The presence and type of secretion depend on the epithelial lining and individual anatomy.

What Is the Crusting We May See?

When secretions remain exposed to air, water can gradually evaporate, leaving behind a more concentrated material that can dry and form a crust.

In a blind-ending accessory nasal tract, retained secretions may therefore become dry and crusted around the opening.

The appropriate medical term would generally be nasal crusting or crusted secretions, rather than assuming that every visible material is ordinary nasal mucus.

Again, the appearance of crusting alone cannot establish the exact internal anatomy of the tract.

Does a Third Nostril Mean an Extra Nose?

No.

A supernumerary nostril does not represent an additional independent nose or a separate respiratory system.

Even when the accessory opening communicates with the nasal cavity, it is simply an additional external nasal opening associated with the existing nasal structures.

The amount of airflow through it depends on factors such as:

* The diameter of the accessory tract
* Whether the tract is patent
* Its connection with the nasal cavity
* The internal anatomical configuration

A blind-ending tract, on the other hand, does not provide a normal pathway for air to reach the main nasal airway.

Can It Be Treated?

Treatment depends on the individual’s anatomy and symptoms.

An asymptomatic accessory nostril may not necessarily require treatment.

However, surgical correction may be considered when the anomaly produces functional, structural, recurrent local problems, or significant cosmetic concerns.

Before surgical treatment, understanding the anatomy of the accessory tract is important. Clinical examination, nasal endoscopy and appropriate imaging may be used when necessary to determine whether the tract communicates with the nasal cavity or ends blindly.

How Rare Is It?

Supernumerary nostrils are exceptionally rare, and much of the medical literature consists of individual case reports and small case series.

Nevertheless, published reports have documented genuine cases of triple nostrils, confirming that an individual can indeed be born with three external nasal openings.

The rarity of the condition makes each documented case valuable for understanding the developmental anatomy of the nose.

The Important Takeaway

A person can be born with three nostrils, although this is exceptionally rare.

A supernumerary or accessory nostril results from abnormal development of the nasal structures during embryogenesis. The additional opening may communicate with the normal nasal cavity through a narrow tract, allowing some airflow, or it may terminate blindly without communicating with the main airway.

A blind-ending accessory tract is not necessarily an empty cavity. Depending on its epithelial lining, it may contain respiratory-type mucosa or skin-like tissue with associated structures. Secretions may therefore occur, and when drainage is limited or absent, mucus accumulation and nasal crusting may develop in some cases.

Most importantly, a third nostril does not mean an extra nose or an independent respiratory system. It represents an unusual variation in the development of the nasal structures.

Rare does not mean impossible — human embryological development can produce remarkably unusual anatomical variations.

References

2. A case report of triple nostrils – Changgeng Yi Xue Za Zhi, 1994.
3. Supernumerary nostril: A rare congenital deformity – International Journal of Pediatric Otorhinolaryngology, 1998.
